name: Light Brown
lede: Light brown is a plain description rather than a historic color name, and old color dictionaries use it as a gloss for dozens of earthy names from ochre to biscuit.

sections.title: A name that explains others
sections.body:
Light brown has no inventor and no first date. It is brown with a modifier, and the ISCC-NBS naming system of 1955 includes it as one of its named blocks; the swatch here sits 5.8 CIEDE2000 units from that block [8]. A 1927 German RAL standard color and a 2010 online color survey each give a close value, which is how the swatch was settled [8].

What the phrase does in books is more interesting. Paterson's *Dictionary of Colour* uses it to define many older names, among them [[avellaneous]], the light brown of the hazelnut or filbert; [[biscuit]], first recorded as a color in 1884; [[clay]]; savannah; pine, for the wood; suede; and ochre, which it also calls an orangey yellow [1]. [[beige]] is defined there as a light brown or a yellowish grey, a color that fashion keeps renaming camel, taupe, stone or sand [1].

sections.title: How loose the words are
sections.body:
The same dictionary calls two screen colors from the X11 list light brown, Peru and DarkGoldenrod [1]. Topaz is described as the dark yellow or light brown of the gem [1]. The label holds a family of dull, warm, middling colors, not one point in a color space.

Color theorists note the difficulty. Jarman, citing Wittgenstein, writes that brown is a kind of darkened yellow with no light of its own, and that there are more browns than greens [2]. Light brown is that darkened yellow at its lightest.

sections.title: In nature and in art
sections.body:
A nineteenth-century color table reproduced by Baty names "light brown spots on a guinea-pig" and the breast of a hoopoe as examples of its yellowish brown, and gives wood brown as yellowish brown mixed with ash grey [3]. In the Church of Sinai mosaic of the Transfiguration, the tunics of Saints Peter and James are rendered in a light brown and a light purple that turn deep blue where Christ's rays touch them [4].

Pastoureau observes that Italian painters of the late 1500s used fewer true yellows, favoring ivory, beige, straw, russet and light brown [5]. Among pigments, [[ochre]] is the standard light-brown earth, and burnt ochre is glossed as a light brown made by heating [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Light brown is one of the commonest colors in the ColorHub archive: 3,081 of 23,781 paintings, about 13 percent, hold a color near this swatch over at least 5 percent of the canvas [6]. The archive's earliest example is a funerary papyrus from about 1069 BC [6]. Its rate peaks in the fourteenth century, at about 2.4 times the overall rate, and the 1390s are the strongest decade, with 11 of 25 works [6]. Mughal painting holds it in 65 of 168 works, three times the overall rate [6]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the colors are as photographed. In printed books, the phrase *light brown* peaks about 1934 [6].
